title: Strawberry Jam
subtitle: Classic British strawberry preserve
excerpt: Strawberry jam made from fresh strawberries and sugar, set with their natural pectin and a little lemon juice. Makes about five standard jars and keeps for up to a year in a cool cupboard.

recipe.sourceNotes: Strawberry jam is one of the most widely made home preserves in Britain. The technique of using a sugar thermometer or the cold-plate test to check the set point appears in British preserving books from at least the nineteenth century.

recipeTools.notes: A large, wide, heavy-based pan. The surface area helps evaporation and reaching the set point.
For reaching the set point of 105 C.
Five sterilised 340 g jars with lids.

content.text: Strawberry jam is fresh strawberries and white sugar cooked to setting point with a little lemon juice. Strawberries are naturally low in pectin, so getting a firm set requires reaching 105 C and not rushing the boiling stage. The result should be bright red, fruity, and set enough to hold its shape on a spoon. It keeps for up to a year sealed in a cool cupboard.

The day before, or at least 2 hours ahead: combine the strawberries, sugar, and lemon juice in the preserving pan. Stir together, then leave to macerate until the sugar has mostly dissolved and the strawberries have released their juice.
Sterilise the jars and lids: wash in hot soapy water, rinse, then place in an oven at 110 C for 15 minutes. Place two small plates in the freezer for the set test.
Bring the jam to a full rolling boil over a high heat, stirring to prevent it catching. Skim off any foam that rises to the top.

Once boiling rapidly, start checking the temperature. The jam is at setting point when it reaches 105 C on a sugar thermometer. This usually takes 15 to 25 minutes of vigorous boiling after the initial boil begins.

To test without a thermometer, put a teaspoon of jam on a cold plate from the freezer. Leave for 30 seconds. Push it with your finger; if the surface wrinkles and the jam holds its shape, it is at setting point.

Remove from the heat and leave to sit for 5 minutes. This prevents the fruit from floating to the top of the jars. Ladle into the warm sterilised jars, filling to within 5 mm of the top. Seal immediately. Turn the jars upside down for 5 minutes, then right them and leave to cool completely.
